i am writing down how the lending shelf has been working since we moved it beside the east entrance at the Marlowe Community Room in February. the shelf is one metal bookcase, three levels high, with a narrow table beside it for forms and returned games. The room is open on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and the shelf is available during those hours only. On Tuesdays, the door opens at 4:30 and closes at 7:00; Saturday hours are 10:00 to 1:00. I usually arrive about fifteen minutes before the Tuesday opening, though that is my own routine and not a scheduled service. The building's public notice still lists the room hours, not the shelf hours, so people sometimes ask whether they can come in on other days. At present, there is no lending outside the room's listed open times.

The top level holds small-box games and the games that are easiest for younger visitors to reach. The middle level has the larger family games, while the bottom level is for heavier boxes and games with pieces that are kept in separate bags. This arrangement is not based on difficulty. A yellow card on the side of the bookcase says, “Please take one game at a time to the table.” That is meant to keep pieces from being mixed across boxes, particularly when several people are looking at games together. The table is not reserved for shelf use, but on busy afternoons we ask visitors to leave enough room for the lending form and for someone else to set down a box.

There are 38 games on the shelf right now, with a paper inventory in a blue binder underneath the table. Each game has a numbered white sticker on its box, and the same number is written beside its title in the binder. The number identifies the game, not the person borrowing it. Titles are written as printed on the boxes, including punctuation, and editions are noted only when two copies have different rules or contents. For example, we have two copies of Lantern Harbor, one marked “Second Edition” and one without an edition label. The copies have separate numbers, so a borrower can write down which box they took. The inventory also has a short note column for such things as a missing insert or a box that should be handled carefully.

For lending, a visitor writes the date, game number, name, and a way to contact them on the sheet clipped to the binder. The usual loan period is two weeks. There is no fee, and we do not ask visitors to leave an identification card. If someone needs more time, the form has a small extension box to fill in with the new return date; they do not need to explain why. A volunteer checks the sheet before handing over a game, but the check is only to make sure the number and return date are readable. We do not currently take reservations by phone or hold a game for a particular person. One visitor asked whether the shelf could send reminders by text, and I wrote the question in the binder's notes, but we have not set up a reminder system.

1. The return slot is a shallow gray tray on the table's lower shelf. Visitors put the whole game box there, rather than leaving it on the bookcase, so a volunteer can check it before it goes back in place.
2. The return sheet has spaces for the game number and the date it came back. The volunteer initials the line after comparing the sticker with the lending entry.
3. If the return tray is full, leave the game on the table beside the tray and do not put it back on the shelf until it has been checked and entered on the return sheet. This condition matters because a few boxes look alike, and an unchecked return can otherwise be mistaken for a game that is ready to lend.
4. A visitor who returns a game when no volunteer is at the table should write the date on the yellow note beside the tray. The volunteer checks that note at the next opening.
5. Pieces that are already bagged should stay in their bags while the volunteer checks the box. We do not count every card during an ordinary return, but we do look for the labeled bags and the rule booklet.

We have had two reports of small pieces being absent, and both were found later in the same game boxes, inside the folded rule sheets. Neither report was written up as a confirmed loss. The binder note asks the next borrower to tell a volunteer if a bag is open or if a piece appears to be missing before taking the game away. This is a request, not a requirement to inspect every component at the table. I have seen people do a quick check, and I have also seen people rely on the note from the previous return. We do not have a standard checklist for every title, because some games have hundreds of cards and tokens and the time needed would vary a lot.

There are three games with current handling notes. Moss Market has a lid that does not stay shut, so its pieces are in a tied cloth bag inside the box. North Line has a folded map with a small tear at one edge; the note says to unfold it on the table rather than pull it open by the torn corner. The third game, Lantern Harbor Second Edition, has a replacement blue marker in a small envelope taped to the inside of the lid. The envelope is not part of the original contents. If that copy is borrowed, the volunteer points out the envelope when checking the number, and the borrower is asked to return it in the same place. These notes are also copied in the binder, because a loose card beside a box is easy to miss when the shelves are busy.

The shelf gets its stock from donations and from purchases paid for through the room's small activities budget. Donation games are not put out as soon as they arrive. A volunteer first checks that the box is clean enough to handle, looks for the rules, and compares the listed pieces with what is in the box when a component list is available. Sometimes the box has no list, so the volunteer writes down what is present without calling the contents complete. We have kept two donated games in a labeled crate under the table while we decide whether their missing rules can be replaced. They are not included in the count of 38 and cannot be borrowed. The crate label says “Review before shelving,” and it has the date the games were received.

At the Saturday opening last week, a parent asked whether children could borrow without an adult's name on the form. I said that the current sheet asks for a name and contact method, and I did not tell them that the rule had changed. The parent wrote down the question but did not take a game. Another visitor asked if there was a list of games suitable for a short session. We have no such list, though a few boxes show an approximate playing time on the front. I usually point to those labels when asked, but I say that the printed time is only an estimate and does not include learning the rules. The shelf has no age-based lending restriction posted, and I have not been given a separate policy about one.

our lighting crew at the bellwether room is small, four people when everyone is available, and the room itself is a converted upstairs hall with a low grid and a narrow loading stair. mara is the production electrician, jo runs the board, and ellis and i handle fixtures and cable; i am usually the person who keeps the paper notes, though jo sometimes takes that job when i am on the ladder. we do not have a separate storage room, so the road cases live behind the black traveler until a visiting company needs that corner. the arrangement is workable, but moving a case through the room can become a little awkward once the audience chairs are set.

this spring we are preparing a revival of the play the glass orchard, which uses twelve conventional fixtures, six led units, two practical lamps and a small haze machine. the director, lena vale, wants the kitchen to feel warm without making the orchard scenes look orange. jo described the early palette as “a little honeyed, but not syrupy,” and we have been using that phrase when we compare the rehearsal looks. the script has three scene changes that happen in near darkness, and the cast cross the upstage platform during two of them. because the platform edge is only marked with low glow tape, the first rehearsal showed that a bright side special could make the tape disappear from the actors’ view. we lowered that special and noted the change on the plot, although the final level is still a choice for the next cue-to-cue.

our hang schedule has to fit around the acting company, who rehearse in the hall most afternoons. we can get ladders into the room on monday and wednesday mornings, and the building manager has asked us not to leave anything across the east fire door overnight. mara wants all overhead fixtures hung and safety-checked before the first focus session; that is a firm part of the plan, not a preference. if the dimmer rack has not been powered for at least twenty minutes before jo checks the led addresses, we will postpone that address check rather than rush it. the rack has behaved normally so far, but its display takes a while to settle after a cold start. we have told the stage manager, dev, that the schedule may shift by half an hour if that condition comes up.

1. before the first ladder goes up, ellis checks each cable for a damaged jacket and puts any questionable lead on the marked shelf by the booth. he writes the fixture number on a strip of masking tape, but the tape is only a temporary label and not a substitute for the proper color code. i enter the fixture number and its position into the paper plot, then jo checks that the channel assignment is the same in the console file. in the last room we worked, we found one lead with a split near the connector, so we are perhaps slightly more cautious about inspecting the ends than we were at the start of the season. the damaged lead is not part of this production’s inventory, and nobody has suggested using it.

2. focus is done with the actors out of the room where possible, because a quiet hall makes it easier to hear the spotter and keeps people clear of the ladders. mara calls the shutter and tilt adjustments; the person at the desk changes the channel only after she confirms the fixture number. on tuesday, jo thought a lantern was aimed at the orchard bench, but it was actually the neighboring unit, which had a similar angle from the floor. we stopped, read both labels, and corrected the plot before carrying on. it did not alter the cue order, though it took longer than we had allowed. the director watched the last part of that focus and said, “I can see the leaves now, but I still want the table to be the first thing you notice.” we have not yet decided whether that means a lower level on the leaf break-up or a small change to the table special.

3. the practical lamps are supplied by the props department, not our crew, and they need to be in their final positions before we finish the stage-right circuits. if props changes the lamp positions after that point, we will recheck the cable path and the shadows on the wall before the next run. this condition matters because one lamp sits close to the legs of the upstage platform, where a loose cable could be hard to see during a dark change. dev has asked props to keep the plug end facing the wall, although we have not yet seen the lamps set in place. until they are there, we can test the outlet and leave the circuit labelled, but we cannot confirm the final look of the practicals. our notes say that plainly so nobody mistakes an empty rehearsal position for a completed focus.

we are keeping the paperwork simple because there is no production electrician assigned for the second week of performances. the current plot has a page for each area, a separate list of borrowed equipment, and a cue sheet with the rehearsal names rather than just the cue numbers. that makes it easier for the person covering jo to follow the conversation at the desk. the borrowed equipment list includes two floor pockets from the studio next door and a short length of black border; the studio manager wants both returned by the friday after closing. mara has put the return date on the outside of the case, and i have also written it in the notebook. this is perhaps more reminder than we need, but borrowed items have gone missing between rooms before, and the studio is using those pockets the following week.

at the end of each work session, ellis coils the spare cable, jo saves the console file under the date and rehearsal name, and i photograph any plot changes that are not yet transferred to the clean copy. we leave the work lights on for the building staff and switch off the practical tests at the wall, since those lamps are not on the lighting desk. if we have used haze, the stage manager opens the hall doors for a few minutes after the actors have left; the building manager asked us not to run the machine during the afternoon classes. we have not needed to use haze in rehearsal yet, so the cleanup note is there for later rather than a record of something already done.

on the next cue-to-cue, we will check the dark changes with the cast moving at their usual pace, then look at the platform edge from the front row and from the stage-right entrance. lena may ask for another adjustment to the orchard look, and i think that is likely, but the current notes do not show a new level yet. if the side special still makes the glow tape hard to see, we will lower it again or test a different angle before the cast repeat the crossing. we also need to confirm the practical lamps after props places them, and to check that the borrowed floor pockets are still clear of the route to the east fire door. until those checks happen, the focus record remains a working copy, with the open choices marked for the next session.

We are at Cedar Bend Orchard on June 14 to repair the irrigation line serving the east bench and Block Three. The crew arrived at 6:40 and walked the lower service road before moving any equipment. The ground was firm near the pump shed but still soft below rows twelve through sixteen from the overnight shower. We found water running across the gravel beside the flush box and a shallow sink forming under the second crossing. The leak was not at the pump itself. The pump was cycling normally, and the supply gauge held at 31 psi while the downstream branch was isolated.

Lena Ortiz met us at the gate and showed where the water first appeared after the morning irrigation run. She said, “We heard a hiss around five, but the rows were already wet, so we could not tell whether it was a broken line or a loose flush cap.” The cap was dry when we checked it, and the water trail began about nine feet east of the box. The line runs beneath the track there and turns toward the old pear rows. The access map calls that turn Junction E3, but the paint mark on the ground is almost gone. We set two cones outside the track and asked the tractor operator to use the north lane until the repair was finished.

For the parts sheet, record the damaged fitting as a four-inch butterfly valve with a cracked downstream flange. The body is still in place, and the handle moves, but water sprays from the flange when the branch is opened. The replacement in the truck is a four-inch wafer-style butterfly valve rated for this line. The flange gasket is also split on its lower edge and needs replacement. The pipe is black polyethylene with a four-inch outside diameter, and the repair will use the two stainless backing rings kept in the blue parts bin.

Tomas Reed was beside the trench and started directing the work as the crew lead. Lena is the orchard manager, and Tomas is the crew lead. Lena authorized access to the east bench, and Tomas coordinated the isolation and digging. No fruit trees were cut, and the nearest trunk is eleven feet from the excavation edge. The trench is about thirty inches deep, with a narrow shelf along the south wall. We used the hand auger to check for roots before widening it and found one small root that we left undisturbed. The soil around the fitting was wet, but there was no standing water below the pipe.

We closed the east bench branch at the manifold and tagged the handle before loosening the union. Tomas waited until the gauge fell to zero, then opened the small drain at the low point to release the remaining water. The north bench stayed on irrigation throughout the repair. The crew supported both sides of the pipe with timber blocks before removing the damaged valve. The flange had two hairline cracks, and the gasket had folded inward near the bottom. There were no cracks in the pipe itself. We cleaned the pipe ends with a lint-free cloth and checked them for grit before fitting the new gasket and valve. The arrow on the valve body points toward the rows and matches the direction marked on the pipe.

1. Check that the branch is isolated and the gauge reads zero before taking the flange apart.
2. Keep the pipe supported while the old valve and gasket are removed.
3. Wipe both mating faces and inspect them for grit or raised edges.
4. Center the replacement valve and gasket before tightening the bolts.

The family photo catalogue brings together images from the Mercer family’s boxes, albums, envelopes, and a small group of digital files. It covers gatherings from 1948 through 2019, with the largest clusters documenting summer visits to Lake Erie, birthdays at the Cedar Street house, and Sunday dinners hosted by Ruth and Daniel Mercer. The catalogue is meant to help relatives find and understand photographs, not to rank them or decide which memories matter most. Each entry identifies what can be seen, gives the best available date and location, and notes who supplied the image or information.

The oldest photographs are mostly black-and-white prints mounted in three albums that belonged to Ruth’s parents. Their handwritten captions include names, dates, and occasional place names, although the writing is not always easy to read. The catalogue retains a transcription when the wording is clear and marks uncertain readings with a question mark. A note beside a photograph dated 1952 reads, “Mildred and the cousins after the rain.” No one has established which cousins are shown, so the entry identifies Mildred and describes the remaining people without assigning names. The photograph’s paper frame gives the date a little more support than the caption alone.

Later collections include loose colour prints, photo-booth strips, slides, and several folders of phone pictures. Many loose prints were originally grouped by event, but a few envelopes have no writing and may have been mixed during a house move. The catalogue records the envelope and box in which each item was found when that detail is available. Digital copies retain their original filenames in a separate field, while catalogue entries use a consistent family-friendly title. This makes the images easier to browse without hiding the names that came with them.

The catalogue uses a small number of practical conventions. Dates can be exact, approximate, or unknown; a month or season is included when it is more reliable than a guessed day. Locations are recorded at the level supported by the evidence, such as “Cedar Street kitchen” or “near Toledo,” rather than being made more precise for neatness. A person’s name is included only when someone can identify the person or a caption supplies the name. If relatives disagree, both accounts are recorded with their sources instead of choosing one by default. These conventions keep the entries readable while leaving room for later corrections.

1. Each entry has a catalogue number, a short title, a date or date range, a location, and a description of the visible scene. The source field identifies an album, envelope, donor, or digital folder whenever that information is known. A separate people field lists confirmed names and notes uncertain identifications. The catalogue number stays attached to the image even if its title or date changes, so printed references and family messages remain useful after an edit.

2. Scans are stored as archival files and as smaller copies for the family’s shared browsing folder. The archival copy keeps the full image area, including borders, handwritten notes, and marks on the back when those details are relevant. A crop may be made for a display page, but it does not replace the uncropped scan. The entry links both versions and notes when a crop has been used. Slide scans are also linked to a record of the original slide mount, since a handwritten label on the mount may provide information that is not visible in the projected image.

3. The catalogue keeps a record of its working notes in the file named below. That record lists questions that remain open, explains changes to names or dates, and gives the date of each edit. A family member can therefore see why an entry changed without having to compare successive copies by eye.

north-gate-notes.md

4. Access is arranged by collection rather than by a blanket rule for every image. Relatives can browse the family folder, while scans that show private correspondence or sensitive personal details are kept in a restricted folder. If a photograph’s location is uncertain and the image could reveal a private home address, the entry stays out of the shared browsing folder until that location has been checked. The catalogue can still retain a restricted record of the image and the reason for the temporary limit. This condition is important because several street photographs look similar, and an old caption may refer to a person’s home rather than the place where the picture was taken.

5. Corrections are added with enough context to be useful. If someone recognizes a person, the entry records who supplied the identification and when it was received. If two relatives remember an event differently, their accounts remain attached to the entry as separate notes. A corrected spelling can replace an earlier transcription when the evidence is clear, while the edit history retains the former spelling. New scans are checked against the physical print when possible, especially if a mark, reflection, or faded face is difficult to distinguish in the digital copy.

The catalogue’s main browsing views group pictures by year, event, location, and confirmed people. Those views are generated from the entry fields, so the same photograph can appear in more than one useful place without making duplicate records. A family member looking for a particular reunion can browse by event, while someone researching a house can browse by location. Unknown dates remain visible in a separate undated group rather than being quietly assigned to a nearby year. The catalogue also includes a short explanation of its date labels, so “about 1960” is not mistaken for a precise date.

The Mercer relatives have contributed information in different ways. Elena Mercer scanned the albums and supplied the box locations; Thomas Mercer identified several people from the Cedar Street dinners; and Priya Shah shared a folder of photographs made during visits with the family between 2008 and 2019. These contributions appear in the source fields, but they do not turn a personal recollection into a confirmed fact. For example, Thomas remembers one picnic as taking place in July, while the album page gives only the year. The entry keeps the year as its catalogue date and records his recollection as a note rather than presenting July as settled.

The catalogue is updated when a relative supplies a scan, a caption becomes legible, or new information changes an entry. Before a group of new pictures is added, the person maintaining the catalogue checks for duplicates and records where the files came from. A duplicate scan may be linked to the existing entry if it shows the same print at better resolution; it is not given a second catalogue number merely because it arrived in another folder. The accompanying note explains what changed, leaving the family with a useful record of both the images and the information gathered around them.

Some photographs remain unidentified, and that is an ordinary part of the collection rather than a reason to fill in a guess. An entry can describe clothing, setting, visible objects, and the arrangement of people while leaving names blank. Relatives who later recognize a face can add information with a source and a date, and a question can remain open if the evidence is still inconclusive. In this way, the catalogue provides a clear route through several generations of photographs while respecting the difference between what an image shows, what a caption says, and what family members remember.

we need a readable account of received volume, plus anything the shift leads ought to inspect in the register or paper slips. We have been maintaining the family photo importer since Aunt Lena asked us to move the scans from her old laptop into the shared archive, and I want to explain what changed during the last two weekends because the next test depends on the folder rules we settled on. The importer reads JPG and JPEG files from an incoming folder and copies them into year and month folders using the date in the image. When that date is missing, it uses the file date but marks the record for review. The original scan stays in the incoming folder until the copy has been checked, and this matters because some of the oldest prints have no reliable date and nobody wants a guessed date to look certain.

On Saturday, I used the small blue USB drive from the hall drawer and copied 214 scans into a test folder on the desktop. The number is the count of source files, not the number of photos, because four files were duplicate scans and one was a text note from Grandpa. The importer skipped the note after checking its extension, but it kept both copies of each duplicate since their filenames were different. The test computer is called Maple and runs Windows 11. The archive share is mounted as Family Archive and has folders through 2023. The newly scanned boxes are from 1987, so we expected the importer to create a 1987 folder and leave later years untouched.

Mara looked at the preview on Sunday and said, “I can tell which pictures need a date, but I cannot tell whether the importer has actually kept the untouched scan.” That is the reason I asked for a visible original status in the preview rather than a second color or another warning symbol. The screen is already busy on her smaller monitor, and she reads it at 125 percent zoom. I tried a green dot first, but she thought it meant the file had been uploaded, so we took the dot out and kept the plain words “original present” beside the filename. The wording is a little dry, but it answers her question without pretending the date is known.

The folder rule needs a careful test because some cameras wrote dates in local time, and some scanners added the day the scan happened instead of the day the photo was taken. The box marked “summer trip” has pictures from two different summers, so its handwritten envelope is useful but not enough to assign every image a year. We agreed that an uncertain date stays uncertain and that the importer should put that item in the review list, not quietly choose the nearest year. When the recorded month is missing, it should still use a known year and put the file in that year folder with “month unknown.” If the year itself is missing, the file stays in incoming until a person can check the envelope.

For the next test, I wrote down the steps in order:
1. Make a fresh copy of the test folder and do not work on the only scan.
2. Open settings and confirm that
archive.retain_originals
is true.
3. Import the 1987 box and note how many files are copied and how many are flagged for review.
4. Open the preview at normal zoom and then at 125 percent to check that “original present” stays readable.

the second-shift note was added at 10:31 by Niko Vale. it says that the sample sleeve is still in the upper drawer and that the comparison lamp had not yet been returned. the logbook was returned to the rack outside the dye room at 10:38, with recipe card revision C still clipped inside the cover. the separate traveler stayed with the finished roll and showed the same batch number, T-241, and the same roll group, G-18. the loose ends of the white thread were put in the waste bin, and the sample sleeve was left in the cabinet drawer as recorded. no laboratory result, shade approval, or later rinse entry appears on this page. the final recorded production condition is that the cloth is wound and the sample is awaiting a daylight check, with the conductivity result below the stated point for requesting another rinse.
